topic: The Mirror World of Graphs: Duality and Euler’s Formula
target_audience: Undergraduate Computer Science or Mathematics students

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Planar Landscape
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a Planar Graph (a graph that can be drawn without edges crossing). Define the three components: Vertices (V), Edges (E), and Faces (F). Introduce Euler’s Characteristic Formula: V - E + F = 2. Visually demonstrate these components using a simple 2D shape.
sections.example: An animation of a 2D 'House' graph: 5 vertices (corners), 6 edges (lines), and 3 faces (the inside of the square, the triangle roof, and the infinite outside area). V(5) - E(6) + F(3) = 2.

sections.title: The Birth of the Dual Graph
sections.content: Introduce the concept of 'Duality' as a transformation. Explain that every planar graph has a 'shadow' or 'dual' version. The transformation rule is: every face in the original graph becomes a vertex in the dual graph.
sections.example: Imagine a map of three neighboring animal territories (Lion, Zebra, Giraffe). We place a 'Guardian' (new vertex) in the center of each territory and one in the 'Great Beyond' (the outer face).

sections.title: The Bridge: Connecting the Dual
sections.content: Explain the mechanics of creating edges in the dual graph. For every edge in the original graph that separates two faces, draw a dual edge connecting the two corresponding dual vertices. Emphasize that the number of edges remains identical (E = E*).
sections.example: The 'Guardian' of the Lion territory wants to talk to the Zebra guardian. They build a 'bridge' (dual edge) that crosses exactly one 'fence' (original edge) separating their lands.

sections.title: Mathematical Symmetry & Euler's Swap
sections.content: Reveal the beautiful symmetry between the original graph (G) and its dual (G*). Show that the number of vertices in the dual equals the faces of the original (V* = F), and the faces of the dual equals the vertices of the original (F* = V). Substitute these into Euler’s formula to show it still equals 2.
sections.example: A split-screen animation showing the 'House' graph. Left side: V=5, E=6, F=3. Right side (Dual): V*=3, E*=6, F*=5. Both satisfy the formula, proving the dual is also a valid planar graph.

sections.title: Application: Mazes and Circuitry
sections.content: Explain why this matters in the real world. In circuit board design, duality helps simplify wiring. In game design, duality is used to generate mazes where the 'walls' are the original graph and the 'paths' are the dual graph.
sections.example: Show a character (a Mouse) navigating a maze. The 'Walls' form a tree graph, while the 'Path' the mouse takes is the Dual Graph. If the walls have no loops, the path is guaranteed to reach the exit.
